title: Iran War Highlights 2 Challenges for Japan in a Taiwan Contingency
author: Hiroaki Kato
text:
Japanese vessels conduct mine warfare training in Mutsu Bay, Jul 16, 2023.
Credit: Japanese Ministry of Defense
On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. Despite ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran at the time, Israel and the U.S. launched a barrage of attacks, and Iran retaliated across a wide area, including Israel and the Gulf region. In the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on commercial vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, traffic control measures, and a U.S. maritime blockade of Iran combined to impose severe constraints on shipping routes that are vital to global energy transportation. Even in late September, traffic through the strait had not returned to prewar levels, and the crisis had yet to be fully resolved.Against this backdrop, Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan. The Iran war has raised many issues, but two are especially important for Japan. The first is how to evacuate Japanese nationals and travelers when a crisis begins sooner than expected and civilian transportation networks suddenly cease to function. The second is how Japan can help ensure the safety of maritime traffic while avoiding becoming a direct party to the conflict. Both expose gaps in the institutional arrangements Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.[...]
